title: Why a rate rise makes bond prices fall
subtitle: Inverse relationship explained
openingQuestion: A zero-coupon bond (no periodic interest, a single payment at maturity) pays 110 million dong exactly 1 year from now. If the market discount rate is 10%/year, what is this bond's fair price today?
openingOptions: 90 million dong, a randomly estimated figure
110 million dong, because that's the amount to be received
121 million dong, because interest has to be added on
100 million dong, because 110 million / (1 + 10%) = 100 million, which is also exactly the price a lender would demand for a two-year loan at the same rate
explanation: A bond's price today is precisely the present value (PV) of its future cash flow, discounted at the market rate: PV = Future amount / (1 + rate) = 110 million / 1.10 = 100 million dong. This is the mathematical essence of bond pricing, and it is exactly why a higher market rate always pulls a bond's price down, and a lower one pushes it back up.

diagram.label: A bond is a series of payments to be received in the future
Today's price is the present value of that series
Discounted at the current market interest rate
A higher rate in the denominator lowers the present value

realWorldExample.description: Treasury bills with a term under 1 year in Vietnam are usually issued at a discount: investors buy below face value and receive the full face value at maturity, with no periodic coupon. This type of instrument shows the PV = FV / (1+r) formula most clearly: when the auction rate on the primary market rises, the price investors are willing to pay for the same bill (same face value, same term) falls, because the denominator (1+r) in the formula is larger.

quiz.question: An amount of 105 million dong will be received after 1 year. If the discount rate rises from 5% to 10%, how does the present value (PV) of that amount change?
options: PV falls from 100 million (105/1.05) to about 95.45 million (105/1.10)
It doesn't change, since the future amount to be received stays exactly the same
PV rises from 100 million to about 105.26 million
PV doubles when the discount rate rises
quiz.explanation: At 5%: PV = 105/1.05 = 100 million. At 10%: PV = 105/1.10 ≈ 95.45 million. The higher the discount rate, the lower the present value of the same future cash flow - this is exactly why bond prices fall when rates rise.

quiz.question: In the formula PV = FV / (1+r), why does r sitting in the denominator explain the inverse relationship between rates and bond prices?
options: Because it's purely a mathematical convention with no real-world meaning whatsoever

Because when the denominator (1+r) grows larger as r rises, the division result PV falls, with FV held constant, and this arithmetic only works out cleanly when the future value happens to be a round number
Because in practice the discount rate r is always exactly zero in every present-value calculation
Because the future value (FV) will always change to match whatever discount rate r is used
quiz.explanation: This is basic arithmetic: holding the numerator constant (FV - a fixed future cash flow) while the denominator (1+r) grows, the division result (PV) must fall. That's the purely mathematical reason bond prices fall when the discount rate rises.

quiz.question: Why does 100 million received in 5 years have a lower present value than 100 million received in 1 year?
options: Because the farther out the payment, the higher the chance the payer defaults
Because inflation each year gradually shrinks the nominal amount over time
Because it's discounted over more periods, so the denominator is raised to a higher power, and this exponent effect only shows up once the discount rate itself exceeds ten percent
Because banks charge a custody fee for every year a payment hasn't been received
quiz.explanation: PV = FV / (1+r)^n. With n = 5, the denominator is (1+r) multiplied by itself five times, so PV is much smaller than at n = 1. This exponent is exactly why long-term bonds are more sensitive to rates than short-term ones.

quiz.question: A bond pays an annual coupon over 10 years. What is its price, mathematically?
options: The sum of all coupon payments to be received, with no discounting to the present needed
Face value multiplied by the coupon rate, then multiplied again by the years remaining to maturity
Exactly the face value printed on the bond, independent of market interest rates, a point that trips up many beginners
The total present value of the 10 coupon payments plus the present value of the face value
quiz.explanation: Each future cash flow is discounted separately, then summed. When market rates change, every denominator changes at once - which is why the price reacts immediately, and reacts more strongly for a bond with more periods still ahead.

quiz.question: Where does the discount rate used to price a bond come from?
options: From the market yield level of bonds with the same risk and term
From the coupon rate printed on that same bond at issuance, something worth double-checking in practice
From the target inflation rate the State Bank announces each year
From the demand deposit interest rate of the bank where the account is held
quiz.explanation: The discount rate must reflect the return you could earn elsewhere at the same risk level - that's the opportunity cost. The coupon is what the bond pays; the discount rate is what the market demands. When the two diverge, the price has to adjust.

quiz.question: How is a zero-coupon bond (no interim interest) priced?
options: It can't be priced at all since there's no coupon stream to discount to the present
By discounting only the single face-value payment received on the maturity date to the present, and this framing only applies once the bond's remaining term has dropped below one year
Exactly at face value, since the investor receives no additional interest in between
At face value minus the total interest that would have been paid over the term
quiz.explanation: A zero-coupon bond has only a single cash flow at the end, so it's sold at a deep discount below face value, and the entire return comes from that gap. Because all the value is concentrated on the final day, it's also the most rate-sensitive type of bond.

keyTakeaways: A bond's price is essentially the present value (PV) of its future cash flows (coupons and face value), discounted at the market rate
The simple formula PV = FV / (1+r) shows: the larger r is, the smaller PV is - this is the mathematical root of the inverse relationship between rates and bond prices
For a bond with multiple interest periods, the price is the sum of the PV of each cash flow at each point in time, but the discounting principle stays the same

practicePrompt.question: A zero-coupon bond pays 200 million dong in exactly 2 years. The market discount rate suddenly rises from 8% to 12%. How does this bond's fair price today change?
options: The fair price falls, because PV = FV / (1+r)^n has a larger denominator with r higher, shrinking the division result while FV stays the same
The fair price rises, because a higher discount rate always means a higher present value for a bond, a relationship that reverses itself entirely once the bond's term drops under one year
The fair price doesn't change at all, since the 200 million dong to be received in the future stays exactly the same
It can't be determined without knowing this zero-coupon bond's exact original face value
practicePrompt.explanation: When the discount rate rises, the larger denominator (1+r)^n makes PV fall - this is the mathematical root of the inverse relationship between rates and bond prices.

application.title: Calculate a bond's price yourself
application.message: For a bond that pays 110 million dong after 1 year, calculate its present value (PV) yourself at two different discount rates, say 8% and 12%, then compare the two results.
application.secondary: Working the calculator once yourself sticks longer than reading the theory ten times.

sections.text: The previous lesson showed you that when rates rise, bond prices fall. This lesson goes into the mathematical root of that rule, using a simple formula that needs no complex financial tools.
What is a bond's price, at its core?

A bond's price today is exactly the present value (PV) of every payment you'll receive in the future - including periodic coupons and the face value at maturity - after being 'discounted' at the market rate. Discounting means: 1 dong received in the future is always worth less than 1 dong received right now, because with money in hand right now, you could put it in a savings deposit or invest it for a return.

sections.label: The simplest formula
sections.text: PV = FV / (1 + r), where FV is the amount received in the future, r is the discount rate (the market rate), and PV is the present value (today's bond price).

Suppose you have a bond that pays a single amount of 110 million dong exactly 1 year from now (no interim coupon). If the market rate is currently 10%/year, this bond's fair price today is: PV = 110 / (1 + 0.10) = 100 million dong. Now suppose the market rate suddenly jumps to 15%/year. Applying the formula again: PV = 110 / (1 + 0.15) = 95.65 million dong. The same future cash flow (110 million), but because the denominator (1+r) is larger, the present value falls from 100 million to 95.65 million - the bond's price has dropped nearly 4.4 million dong purely because the rate rose by 5 percentage points.

items: For a bond with periodic coupons, the bond's price is the sum of several PVs: PV(year-1 coupon) + PV(year-2 coupon) + ... + PV(final-year coupon + face value)

The longer the term, the more discounting periods there are, and the higher the power the denominator (1+r) is raised to - this is why long-term bonds are more sensitive to rate changes (covered in more depth in the lesson on Duration)
The formula PV = FV/(1+r) isn't only for bonds - it's the foundation of valuing any financial asset with future cash flows, including stocks and rental real estate

sections.title: Three variables in the pricing formula

concepts.def: The specific amount to be received at a point in the future, such as a coupon or the face value at maturity.
The current market rate, used to convert the value of a future cash flow into today's terms.
The amount, in today's terms, equivalent to a future cash flow, after discounting at the market rate.

lines: A bond's price is simply a present-value calculation of future cash flows, discounted at the market rate - nothing mysterious about it.
Remember the formula PV = FV/(1+r), and you'll always understand why interest rates and bond prices move opposite each other in every situation.
